source_text: Verum nunc, quod locus exigit, insequamur. Apparet te, subtilissime disputator, unam eamdemque rem, naturam scilicet humanam magnis extulisse laudibus, sed maioribus maculasse criminibus; quod sicut uno tempore, uno opere, unoque consilio evenire simul non potest; ita ratio naturalis nequaquam capit haec, vel sub alternatione contraria, sed uno semper plena, id est, taxatione boni, numquam propter malum, quod eius instituta per actoris sui non capiunt dignitatem, nisi a pollutissimo Manichaeorum dente mordetur. Sed hoc expleto, illud inquiro, quos putes connubii fumos sequendos. Nam si connubium fateris non esse causam hominis, sed naturam; peccati quoque causam non esse connubium, sed naturam; hoc connubium, cui laudem dabas, totum prorsus evanuit. Cui ergo rei adscribitur, si nec mali tui, nec boni mei causa est? Si ab honestate connubii hominem submoves, ne eum etiam fornicationi cogaris adscribere; a necessitate connubii peccatum removes, ne nuptias damnare videaris; quid remansit laude dignum in possessione coniugii? Cur illud times violare sermone, quod admota disputatione funditus subruisti? Cuius ergo rei causa esse dicetur, si nec malo nec bono participat naturali? Nihil ergo iam agit in rebus humanis nomen honestasque coniugii? Sed angeris, et dure quidem; subveniendum est igitur anhelo seni. Remansit quod ei dare possis, sine quo tamen nihil aliud invenitur; videlicet ut dicas hoc connubium stare pro foribus, ut ad voluptatem coeuntium nullam obscenitatis famam permittat irruere, sed suo titulo illi negotio honestatem vindicet et pudorem. Sine causa ergo connubii fidem subdola corrumpere laude voluisti; nulli est infestius, quam tibi. Vos omnino proturbat, nec ad lacerationem commixtionis tutelae suae creditae, Manichaeorum linguas permittit irrepere. Habent, inquit, suo dogmate digna meritoria, in quibus nocturnis horis expleantur; illam verecundantium voluptatem connubii tuentur excubiae, arcentur crimina, et honor honestatis admittitur; privilegia sibi ab Apostolo concessa defendunt honorabiles nuptias et thoros immaculatos; fornicatores autem et adulteros iudicabit Deus [n56] . Ubi est ergo criminosa commixtio, si negotio eius atque secreto auctoritas connubii, quod laudabas, obsequitur?
pass_a_gloss: But now, what the place demands, let us pursue. It appears that you, most subtle disputant, have lifted one and the same thing, namely human nature, with great praises, but have stained it with greater charges; which as it cannot happen together at one time, by one work, and by one counsel; so natural reason by no means takes these, even under a contrary alternation, but always full of one thing, that is, of the assessment of good, never on account of evil, which its institutions do not take through the dignity of its actor, unless it is bitten by the most polluted tooth of the Manichaeans. But this having been fulfilled, I inquire whom you think the smokes of wedlock to be followed. For if you confess that wedlock is not the cause of the human, but nature; that the cause of sin also is not wedlock, but nature; this wedlock, to which you were giving praise, has altogether vanished. To what thing therefore is it ascribed, if it is the cause neither of your evil nor of my good? If you remove the human from the honorableness of wedlock, lest you be compelled to ascribe him also to fornication; you remove sin from the necessity of wedlock, lest you seem to condemn marriages; what has remained worthy of praise in the possession of marriage? Why do you fear to violate by speech what you have thoroughly undermined by an applied disputation? Of what thing therefore will it be said to be the cause, if it shares in neither natural evil nor good? Does therefore the name and honorableness of marriage already do nothing in human affairs? But you are distressed, and harshly indeed; one must therefore help the panting old man. There has remained what you can give it, without which nevertheless nothing else is found; namely that you say this wedlock stands before the doors, so that it permits no fame of obscenity to rush upon the pleasure of those coupling, but by its title claims honorableness and modesty for that business. Without cause therefore you wanted to corrupt the faith of wedlock by a sly praise; it is hostile to none more than to you. It altogether drives you out, nor does it permit the tongues of the Manichaeans to creep in for the tearing of the mingling entrusted to its protection. They have, it says, lodgings worthy of their dogma, in which they may be fulfilled in nocturnal hours; the watches of wedlock protect that pleasure of those reverencing, charges are kept off, and the honor of honorableness is admitted; honorable marriages and undefiled beds defend privileges granted themselves by the Apostle; but God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Where therefore is the criminal mingling, if the authority of wedlock, which you were praising, obeys its business and secret?

pass_b_english: Let us now pursue what the passage requires. It is clear, most subtle debater, that you have exalted one and the same thing—human nature—with great praises, but stained it with still greater accusations. Just as these cannot occur together at one time, in one work, and under one intention, so natural reason cannot admit them even as alternating opposites. Nature always possesses one full valuation, namely goodness. It is never attacked for evil—which its institutions, because of its maker’s dignity, do not admit—except by the utterly filthy teeth of the Manichaeans.

Having completed this point, I ask what wisps of marriage you think you should pursue. If you confess that the cause of a human being is not marriage but nature, and the cause of sin too is not marriage but nature, then the marriage you were praising has entirely vanished. To what effect is it assigned if it is the cause of neither your evil nor my good? You remove the human being from marriage’s honorable activity lest you be compelled to attribute him to fornication too. You remove sin from marriage’s necessary activity lest you appear to condemn marriage. What remains worthy of praise in marriage’s possession? Why fear to violate with a word what you have utterly demolished by argument? Of what will it be called the cause if it shares in neither natural evil nor natural good? Do the name and honor of marriage now accomplish nothing in human affairs?

But you are choking, and painfully. We must therefore help the panting old man. Something remains you can give marriage, without which nothing else is found: say that marriage stands guard at the door, allowing no report of obscenity to burst in upon the partners’ pleasure, but claiming honor and modesty for that activity under its own title. Your attempt to corrupt marriage’s integrity with deceitful praise was therefore pointless. It is more hostile to no one than to you. It drives you utterly away and does not allow Manichaean tongues to creep in and lacerate the union entrusted to its protection. ‘They have brothels worthy of their doctrine,’ it says, ‘where they may satisfy themselves at night.’ Marriage’s watch guards the pleasure of modest people; crimes are barred and the honor of decency admitted. The privileges the apostle granted defend honorable marriage and undefiled beds; ‘but God will judge fornicators and adulterers’ (Hebrews 13:4). Where, then, is the criminal union, if the authority of the marriage you praised serves its activity and privacy?
